question: How does sugar become an industry — taxed, refined, stored and fought over — in the Islamic and Chinese worlds, and then carried to the Atlantic?
summary: Five centuries turn sugar from a luxury into an organised business. The core of the folio is Egypt, whose Fatimid, Ayyubid and Mamluk states leave the richest records: refineries counted in Fustat, tax offices for raw sugar, sultans who give out thousands of qintars at Ramadan, amirs who build their own presses and a treasurer who is arrested for taxing them ([[ec8]], [[o1]], [[b3]], [[o3]], [[o4]], [[l6]]). The numbers are the point of this folio: for the first time we can see sugar measured in tonnes, dinars, faddans and factories.

Around that core the same pattern repeats in other places: a state or lord wants the revenue, a crop is concentrated on irrigated land, refining moves into specialist hands (Jewish and Karimi merchants in Egypt, the Order of St John and Venetian houses in Cyprus, nobles and merchants in Sicily) and then collapses or moves on when war, plague or politics breaks the chain ([[ec5]], [[ec10]], [[ec11]], [[c3]], [[c4]], [[w2]], [[c1]]). Sugar is also a medicine, a dietary theory and a party food: the folio shows it in sugar-candy dioramas, confectioners' streets and cookbooks ([[e1]], [[e2]], [[e5]], [[t8]]).

China follows a separate track, built around Sichuan candy and a Song-dynasty treatise, then broken by the Mongol invasion ([[ec2]], [[te1]], [[w1]]). The last stage is the Atlantic move: Madeira ships sugar to Portugal, Columbus is a buyer there, and in 1493 he carries cane to Hispaniola ([[ec13]], [[x8]], [[x10]]). Everything the next folios treat as new has an Egyptian, Cypriot or Sicilian precedent in this one.

themes.title: Egypt as the measured economy
text: The Mamluk records let us count: refineries at Fustat, presses on an amir's estate, a raw-sugar store under tax, a sultan's Ramadan allowance rising from 1,000 to 3,000 qintars, and a Mongol raid on 600 loads. The same sources show how the state hunted the revenue, and how it was dodged.

themes.title: Sugar westward: Mediterranean islands as laboratories
text: Sicily, Cyprus, Granada, Valencia and finally Madeira each run the model — royal or noble land, irrigation, imported skills, Italian capital — and each shows how fragile it is: Frederick II's deportation of the island's Muslims, the fall of Acre, the Cypriot king's failed loan, Palermo's rise after tax breaks.

themes.title: Sugar in the body and on the table
text: Physicians from Ibn Butlan to Ibn al-Nafis refine the medical theory of sugar; cooks and confectioners use it for sweets and for meat; Fatimid caliphs make it a show of power. The Song capital's street-sellers and the Yuan court dietitian's recipes show the same drift in China.

themes.title: Who did the work, and who paid
text: Geniza documents show Jewish merchants and physician-entrepreneurs running refineries and shipping sugar; Wang Zhuo says Sichuan villages gave up making sugar sculptures because the powerful demanded all of it; Syrian refugees bring cane know-how to Cyprus; and Buttery's report of Jewish children sent to São Tomé is flagged as unverified.

themes.title: China: Sichuan candy and the Mongol break
text: A Song treatise says only five counties can make sugar candy and gives the proportions of land and households tied to cane at Suining; a stone-drum mill is described; then the Mongol invasion destroys Sichuan's cane economy and the Yuan state tries to rebuild it.

turning_points.text: A sugar-candy banquet with 152 figures is paraded through Cairo: sugar as spectacle.
Wang Zhuo writes the treatise on sugar candy, naming the five counties of China that can make it.
Salah al-Din abolishes miscellaneous taxes, among them those on the raw-sugar store: a glimpse of how sugar was taxed.
Frederick II orders two sugar-makers sent to Palermo: the state hunts for skills.
The fall of Acre ends Latin sugar estates on the Syrian coast; Cyprus becomes the new centre.
Ibn Duqmaq counts 65 refineries at Fustat.
The plague reaches Egypt and begins the long decline of its sugar.
Palermo's cane lands grow tenfold after the Crown grants tax breaks.
Madeira is shipping sugar to Portugal.
Columbus carries cane from the Canaries to Hispaniola.

how_to_read: The folio is large, and the *Economy*, *Order* and *Lives* lanes carry most of the numbers. For Egypt, read *Order* as a sequence (o1 to o5); for the Mediterranean move, follow *Economy* from Almería and Cyprus to Madeira. The *Thought* lane is the medical and dietetic literature, and *Exchange* the networks and routes.

The cross-links to other folios (Fatimid, Mamluk, Cyprus, Norman Sicily) are the way to place a single entry in its wider setting; the Nexus shows the causal chain from the plague and the fall of Acre to the Atlantic.

The *picture by region* counts the 65 entries: Europe 17, Near East 33, Far East 11, Africa 3, Americas 1; none in Oceania or Worldwide. Egypt’s Mamluk and Fatimid states dominate; the Atlantic appears only at the end.

sources.intro: This is the first folio with real numbers, and they come from three main places: a specialist's reading of the Arabic chronicles and administrative texts, a Mediterranean economic historian, and a Chinese economic historian.
main: Sato Tsugitaka, *Sugar in the Social Life of Medieval Islam*, which carries the Egyptian and Syrian material (about thirty entries, including the tax, refinery and Geniza-based entries).
Ouerfelli, *Le sucre*, for Sicily, Cyprus and the western Mediterranean (about eighteen).
Mazumdar, *Sugar and Society in China*, for Sichuan, the Song and Yuan (about eighteen); Needham for the technology.
Goitein's Geniza work for the merchants' documents, through Sato and Ouerfelli.
contested: Marco Polo's account of Fujian sugar-making ([[x4]]).
The Heian gift of 1091, cited by Needham from a Japanese source not read ([[x2]]).
Buttery's report of Jewish children sent to São Tomé ([[l7]]).
The scale of Madeira's early industry and the stories of Sicilian advisers ([[ec13]]).
gaps: No Arabic or Chinese primary texts were read directly; Sato and Mazumdar give the passages.
Deerr's *History of Sugar*, which is the older standard for the Atlantic islands, and a Madeira specialist (Vieira) were not read.

text: Seventeen entries around three Mediterranean islands and the Spanish coast: Almería, Granada’s Almuñécar and Motril, Norman and Hohenstaufen Sicily, Palermo’s cane boom, tax privileges and water decree, Cyprus under Hospitallers and Venetians, Valencia’s first trapig, and the wars that empty Sicily’s cane lands ([[ec1]], [[ec9]], [[ec3]], [[o6]], [[o7]], [[ec11]], [[ec5]], [[ec6]], [[ec10]], [[x6]], [[x7]], [[ec12]], [[c1]], [[x3]], [[te2]], [[te4]], [[t4]]).

Thirty-three entries, the core of the folio, mostly Egypt: refineries, presses, taxes and confiscations, Ramadan grants, banquets and cookbooks, physicians from Ibn Ridwan to Ibn al-Nafis, and the people who work the sugar; plus the Mongol sack on the Harran road, the fall of Acre, Bedouin raids on Upper Egypt, the Black Death, a Fustat merchant’s sugar shipped to Qayrawan and Constantinople’s first sugar trade ([[x1]], [[ec8]], [[ec7]], [[o1]], [[o3]], [[o4]], [[b1]], [[b3]], [[e1]], [[t1]], [[t8]], [[c2]], [[c3]], [[c4]], [[w2]], [[x5]], [[l1]], [[l6]]).

Eleven entries: Sichuan’s candy economy and Wang Zhuo’s ox-driven mill, Kaifeng’s sugar lions and Hangzhou’s honey-boiling office, the Yuan farm manual and dietary manual, Marco Polo’s Egyptian refiners in Fujian, Song sugar given as gifts in Heian Japan, Zhao Rugua’s list of goods sold in Southeast Asia, and the Mongol destruction of Sichuan’s cane ([[ec2]], [[te1]], [[e2]], [[e4]], [[t6]], [[e6]], [[x4]], [[x2]], [[x9]], [[w1]], [[l2]]).
Three entries: Madeira becomes the leading Portuguese supplier, Columbus buys sugar there, and Jewish children are sent to São Tomé ([[ec13]], [[x8]], [[l7]]). The Atlantic move begins here.
One entry, the last of the folio: in 1493 Columbus carries cane from the Canaries to Hispaniola ([[x10]]).
